title: Keep your half of the tally
word: Keep your half of the tally
hookLine: after a great quarrel, some resentment stays; the sage keeps his side of the tally and demands nothing (Tao Te Ching 79)

cards: The fight is over. Apologies were said, maybe even hugs, and everyone agreed to move on. Then, a month later, a small remark lands wrong, and there it is again: the old sting, right where it was.
Making peace and being at peace are two different things. Chapter seventy-nine of the Tao Te Ching starts there, with what's left over after the treaty is signed.
Its first line came up on day nine hundred ninety, about reconciling; today the chapter goes further.

teach.b: First, the leftover. When a great resentment is settled, the chapter says, some resentment is sure to remain. How can that be called good?
Patching things up after a big break doesn't get everything back. Better, the chapter implies, not to pile up the debt in the first place. Second, the tally.
A tally, as commentators describe it, is a record of an agreement split into two halves, one for each side, so the halves can be matched later.
The sage holds his half and makes no demands on the other person. He has the proof; he just doesn't press it. Third, two kinds of people.
Those with virtue look after the tally; those without it look after collecting. One keeps the agreement and lets it rest. The other is always out knocking on doors for what's owed.
Fourth, the last line: heaven's way has no favorites, and it is always with the good person. That pulls the week's thread tight. Heaven's net is loose but loses nothing.
Threats wound the one who holds them. Hunger traces back to those who take too much. Soft is alive.
And today: hold your half, and don't collect. It looks like knowing exactly what someone owes you, and choosing not to send the bill.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-nine as advice on old grievances: settling a great resentment leaves some behind, so the sage keeps his side of an agreement and does not press others for what they owe.

games.q: what does “keep your half of the tally” mean?
o: splitting the bill evenly so both sides pay the same
holding your side of a deal without pressing for payment
counting up every debt so nothing is ever forgotten

games.q: chapter seventy-nine and this week: tap the pairs.

s: chapter seventy-nine says settling a great quarrel clears all resentment
it says some resentment is sure to remain, and asks how that can be called good.
the sage in chapter seventy-nine holds his half of the tally
and makes no demands on the other person.
the chapter says heaven's way plays favorites

games.q: you hold your half of the tally. the other side owes you. what does the sage in chapter seventy-nine do?
o: hold the tally and make no demands.
games.why: the sage keeps his half and demands nothing. those with virtue look after the tally; those without it look after collecting.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've been waiting for someone to give you: an apology, a thank-you, a favor returned, money owed.

You may well be right that it's owed; hold your half of the tally, the knowledge of it, and for these two minutes set the demand down beside you. Notice what the hands, the chest and the jaw do when you stop collecting.

wordCard.voice: Keep your half of the tally. Chapter seventy-nine: the sage holds his half of the agreement and makes no demands on the other. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: the left half of the tally, which the sage holds in chapter seventy-nine.

carryVoice: Your line: demand nothing. The proof can stay in your pocket. Rest well.
